title: What to keep from Thoreau
hook: simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small

segments.voice: Yesterday, prickly and good: Emerson naming how easily Thoreau said no, and loving him anyway. Did you find the good next to someone's sharp edge? Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

A suitcase, and not much room in it. That's roughly where we are with Thoreau. We've walked through a cabin, a bean field, a pond, a jail cell, a mountain, a shoreline, a journal and a sickroom. Tomorrow we leave him. Nobody carries a whole writer out the door. So the question today is a packing question. Out of everything, what goes in the bag? Here are four things readers pick up from him. You only need one.
screen: `A SMALL SUITCASE.` → `WHAT GOES IN THE BAG?` → `FOUR THINGS, KEEP ONE.`

segments.voice: First, simplicity. In Walden he writes, "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" Three times, as if once weren't enough. Fewer things, fewer affairs, so there's room left for a life. Second, wildness. In his essay Walking he writes, "In Wildness is the preservation of the World." Not wilderness only, out there. Wildness: the part of the world, and of a person, that hasn't been tamed into usefulness. We met it on Ktaadn, in his cry of contact. Third, conscience. In his essay on civil government he writes, "I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward." A person before a citizen. Conscience before convenience. That's the night in jail, folded into one sentence. Fourth, attention to the small. This one has no single slogan, because it's everywhere: the ice going out on the pond, the line in the journal, a violet's flowering, the stream he fishes in. This week alone, we watched him turn notebooks into seasons and time into water. And Emerson's teasing phrase fits here too. He was the captain of a huckleberry party. Some might call that small. It might be the whole point. Four doors into the same house. Some readers walk in through simplicity, some through the woods, some through protest, some through a notebook. None is the right one. Thoreau himself wasn't tidy enough to be summed up in one, and his friends would remind you he wasn't easy either. But a person can carry one of these for years.
screen: `SIMPLICITY, SIMPLICITY, SIMPLICITY!` · `IN WILDNESS IS THE PRESERVATION.` · `MEN FIRST, AND SUBJECTS AFTERWARD.` · then, large: `ATTENTION TO THE SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one. Sit, and breathe. Let the four pass by slowly, one per breath. Simplicity. Wildness. Conscience. Attention to the small. Notice which one tugs at you. Not the one you think you should choose. The one that pulls. Then let the other three go, gently, and stay with the one. Ask what it might look like in an ordinary week: one thing given away, one walk in the rain, one honest no, one line in a notebook. The bell holds the time.
What to keep from Thoreau. Simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small: four doors, and you only need one. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT TO KEEP FROM THOREAU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep one. Today, write the one you picked somewhere you'll see it, and do one small thing for it before bed. Day one thousand two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Some people who take something lasting from Thoreau settle on one thread, a simpler life, time in wild places, acts of conscience or close attention to nature, and build a small habit around it.
